entities.name: Ioannis Orlandos
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Ioannis Orlandos, a prominent Hydriot shipowner, politician, and fervent revolutionary, emerged as a pivotal figure in the Greek War of Independence (1821–1829), playing an indispensable role in securing the nascent Greek state's financial viability and diplomatic recognition. Born into a wealthy maritime family on the island of Hydra, then under Ottoman rule, Orlandos leveraged his considerable influence and financial acumen to support the revolutionary cause from its inception. His significance lies not only in his active participation in national assemblies but more crucially in his instrumental efforts to procure foreign loans, which proved vital for sustaining the protracted struggle against the Ottoman Empire and establishing the foundations of modern Greece's economic and political structures.

Orlandos’s contributions were multifaceted, encompassing both military finance and political administration. He served as a representative for Hydra in the First National Assembly at Epidauros (1821–1822), where he helped draft the first Greek Constitution, and subsequently in the Second National Assembly at Astros (1823) and the Third National Assembly at Troezen (1827). His most critical mission, however, came in 1824 when he, along with Andreas Louriotis and Spyridon Trikoupis, was dispatched to London to negotiate two substantial loans from British philhellenic bankers. These loans, totaling approximately £2.8 million (nominal value), provided desperately needed funds for the revolutionary government, enabling the purchase of ships, arms, and provisions, despite the controversial terms and significant deductions that ultimately reduced the net amount received.
